chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
title: Drinks with Coleman Hawkins at the White Rose on 52nd Street
summary: Hawkins, who never bought drinks for others, bought Caldwell drinks and urged him to keep his own style.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Because I know when he was down in 52nd Street before the war, I used to go down there and catch him. So the place called the White Rose, and all of these (unintelligible) 52nd Street would hang playing (unintelligible) in there, and I'd go down (I went up to Ben Webster) there to catch Hawk, and I saw (unintelligible). I said, hey, said, where's Bean? Hawk's down in that White Rose bar. So I said, okay. So I'd go on down to the White Rose bar. Hawk would be way in the back by himself. So I'd go in there and, (( hey, what do you say, old master. Hey, Hap, where you been? 2" " came down to I came see you specifically to hear you play."

He said, you come to hear me play, said, I'm going up to hear you play. I said, well, I'm right here to see you tonight, to be your buddy. He said, that something -- there is another thing about it. He never would buy people drinks, you know. People couldn't understand why he would buy me a drink. So I said, well, Bean, have one on me. No, no, this one's on me. We're buddies from way back. I said, yeah, we're buddies from way back. He said you 211 and he's still playing on them old, funny ideas you got. I said, no, I'm playing what I can find,
create a little something. He said, stay that way. You got a style, I'd say stay that way. You got the tone. Keep it that way. (Unintelligible) you've got the right idea.

Well, (unintelligible) your old funny idea, and the guy upstairs -- I don't understand why you go back there and talk with Hawk and he buy you drinks and he won't buy nobody else. I said, well, I had nothing to do with that. I said, you know, Hawk's the one inspired me on the tenor saxophone.

Well, I don't -- you know, it's a funny thing about that buying the drinks because I know he did, but he would -- I used to, now, I never used to talk music to him. We used to talk about Europe, and we used to talk about cars.
(Simultaneous remarks)

He would buy me a drink. Every now and again, says, time I bought you one. So, you know, I said, fine. And then every now and again, you know, if you didn't force it, he'd come out with something about music, you know. If you said -- if you said you'd been listening to a record today and, you know, then he'd say something, but you couldn't pressure him into --
No, you couldn't.
You know?
I would let him lead all the talking.
That's right.
MR. CALDWELL: He would ask me so and so and so and
about Stump Evans

so, and I (unintelligible), sit down and we talk. I said, give us another little taste (unintelligible). Said, you're always talking about that little taste, me and you and I, we've been together so long. I said, I'm supposed to be (unintelligible) with you. He said, what about me? I'm glad to see you down here with me.
But them other guys, he wouldn't buy them.
(Laughter and simultaneous remarks)
I would buy him drinks.

But he's funny, you know, and -- I said, Hawk, you going home? He said, yeah, Hap, come on. So on the bandstand and blow up 2 I'd go and he'd go (unintelligible) the breeze, and I'd set him up a drink. He said, asked, where that drink come from? I Happy Caldwell, he said, give him said, (unintelligible) giving a return message.
(Laughter)
And them guys couldn't understand why we was this close together.
